hints: Start by comparing each inside concentration in Table 3.1 with the fixed outside concentration of $0.9 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. Where does the difference in height change from negative to positive?
Remember Visking tubing lets water through but not sucrose, so only water can move to even things up. Think about how more sucrose means lower water potential.
Link the direction of net water movement in or out of the tubing to whether the meniscus rises (+) or falls (-), moving down the water potential gradient.
walkthrough:
Spot the Turning Point in the Table**
Look closely at Table 3.1. The outside solution is always $0.9 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ sucrose. For inside solutions of 0.0, 0.4 and 0.8 the change is -12, -4 and -2 mm, so the level fell. For 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0 the change is +1, +6 and +11 mm, so the level rose. The switch happens around 0.9, which tells you the relative concentrations control the direction.

Translate Concentration into Water Potential**
Sucrose lowers water potential. Visking tubing is permeable to water but not to sucrose, so sucrose stays where it is and only water moves. When inside sucrose is less than outside, inside water potential is higher than outside. When inside sucrose is more than outside, inside water potential is lower than outside.

Link Net Water Movement to the Meniscus**
Water always moves by osmosis from higher water potential to lower water potential. So with 0.0 to 0.8 inside, net water leaves the tubing and volume inside drops, so the meniscus falls. With 1.2 to 2.0 inside, net water enters the tubing and volume inside increases, so the meniscus rises.

Final answer: Inside concentrations of 0.0, 0.4 and 0.8 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ are lower sucrose than outside ($0.9 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$), so have higher water potential; net water moves out by osmosis and meniscus falls. Inside concentrations of 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ are higher sucrose than outside, so have lower water potential; net water moves in by osmosis down the water potential gradient and meniscus rises.

hints: Read the axes of Fig. 3.2 carefully and pick out three regions: where the curve is flat at 100%, where it falls steeply, and where it is flat at 0%. Note the concentrations at the bends.
Think about what 100% bursting means for water movement - in which direction must water be moving in very dilute salt solution compared with the inside of the cell?
Remember a red blood cell has only a cell surface membrane with no cell wall to resist expansion, so what happens if a lot of water keeps entering?

Now contrast this with high salt concentrations of about $0.14 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and above where no bursting occurs - what does that tell you about the water potentials being equal or lower outside?
walkthrough:
Describe the Three Parts of the Curve**
Reading Fig. 3.2 with units: at 0.00 to about $0.04 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ sodium chloride, 100% of red blood cells are destroyed. From about 0.04 to $0.14 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ the percentage falls steeply, for example about 80% at 0.06, about 45% at 0.08 and about 28% at $0.10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, reaching 0% at $0.14 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. From $0.14$ to $0.24 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ it stays at 0%.

Explain Bursting in Very Dilute Solution**
Pure water and very dilute salt have a very high water potential, higher than the cytoplasm of the red blood cell. Water therefore moves into the cell by osmosis across the partially permeable cell surface membrane. The cell increases in volume and internal pressure rises.

Why No Wall Means No Survival**
Plant cells can become turgid because the strong cellulose wall resists pressure. Red blood cells have only a thin membrane and no wall, so the membrane cannot withstand the pressure and ruptures. This is haemolysis, giving 100% destruction at $\leqslant 0.04 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

Explain the Fall to Zero Bursting**
As external NaCl concentration rises, external water potential falls. Between 0.04 and 0.14 fewer cells gain enough water to burst. At about $0.14 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and above the outside solution has water potential equal to or lower than the cell, so there is no net movement of water inward. Cells do not swell and burst, and at high concentrations water may even leave, causing shrinkage.

Final answer: At $\leqslant 0.04 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ NaCl, 100% of cells burst; between 0.04 and $0.14 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ percentage bursting falls from 100% to 0%; at $\geqslant 0.14 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ 0% burst. In dilute solutions external water potential is higher than inside, so water enters by osmosis, cells swell and burst (haemolysis) as there is no cell wall. In concentrated solutions external water potential is equal to or lower than inside, so no net entry of water and no bursting; water may leave cells.
